metadata.note: Week 8 report reel. The report-backed claim is observability, not a demonstrated attack: the project now extracts prompt-conditioned OpenVLA attention maps needed to measure a future Attention Magnet Patch.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Ameya Padwad, an AI Engineer, and this video is about making OpenVLA's attention visible. Bella is an AI narrator presenting this work. Before a physical patch can be tested for steering a robot, we need to measure where the model looks when it reads a task instruction. This week adds that measurement.

Three report-backed outputs land: reusable runtime, /attention endpoint, live validation.

props.command: Can we measure where an OpenVLA task prompt attends in a robot camera frame before trying to steer that attention with a physical patch?

beats.narration_text: This is not an attack result yet. It is the observability layer that makes one measurable. The first draft says the model has a heatmap. The correction is that the map comes from a real task prompt reading a real camera frame, so the next experiment can test whether a patch changes it.

beats.narration_text: The new pathway is a real OpenVLA forward pass. A LIBERO camera frame and a task instruction enter the remote model. The extractor selects prompt-token queries, follows their attention to the 256 visual-token keys placed after the beginning token, normalizes that visual mass, and returns one sixteen-by-sixteen map for each selected Llama layer.

show.event: Input nodes land: 224 by 224 LIBERO camera frame and task instruction.
The OpenVLA forward-pass node opens into prompt queries and 256 visual-token keys.
Normalization resolves into per-layer 16 by 16 maps and an averaged map.

props.title: From Prompt To Visual Attention
props.footerNote: 256 visual tokens follow <BOS>; text tokens query them.

beats.narration_text: The important distinction is architectural. OpenVLA uses a decoder-only Llama-2 backbone, not a separate encoder-decoder cross-attention block. Its multimodal sequence inserts vision tokens directly after the beginning token. The reported map is therefore causal self-attention from the prompt's text tokens onto those visual positions, not a generic saliency picture.

show.event: The title establishes the distinction: not encoder-decoder cross-attention.
Three definitions land sequentially: decoder-only backbone, visual keys, and text queries.
The final row states the measured quantity: normalized causal self-attention onto visual tokens.

terms.meaning: Llama-2 uses one causal sequence, not a separate cross-attention block.
256 image tokens are inserted directly after the beginning token.
Prompt tokens place attention mass over those visual-token positions.

beats.narration_text: The live smoke tests make three checks. First, the endpoint returned thirty-two sixteen-by-sixteen maps, covering all thirty-two Llama layers and two hundred fifty-six visual tokens. Second, every layer's normalized map summed to one. Third, repeated requests matched exactly, while changing the instruction produced a non-zero change. That is evidence of prompt-conditioned attention, not a static vision-only signal.

show.event: Executed-test table header appears with the report as its source.
The returned-map row lands: 32 layers, each 16 by 16, covering 256 visual tokens.
The repeatability row lands: maximum difference 0.000e+00.
The changed-instruction rows land: mean difference 1.14e-4 and maximum 2.27e-3.

beats.narration_text: The result is a tested interface for the next security question. The project can now store clean attention baselines, connect them to patch-optimization loops, and test whether attention can be concentrated on a patch as the robot's viewpoint changes. The work does not claim that steering has succeeded. It establishes the measurement needed to judge that claim honestly.

show.event: A result artifact page opens with the completed observability interface.
Three next-step lines enter: clean baselines, optimization-loop connection, changing-viewpoint evaluation.
A final constraint line appears: measurement complete; attack success not claimed.

artifactLines: Boundary: no successful trajectory-steering attack is claimed.

Ask it to propose a repeated-input control, an instruction-swap control, and a measurable pass condition. Then compare that plan with your own model interface before you trust a visualization.
